- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥ 0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–3% for next period.  
- When sentiment is negative (≤ 0.33) or volatile, model often underestimates; adjust upward by 1–2% if recent price is falling.  
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., +5%+ in 3–5 days), model frequently overshoots in subsequent forecasts; apply a “cool-down” correction: subtract 2–5% from forecast 2–3 days after spike.  
- If model forecast is > 20% above recent 7-day average, consider mean reversion bias — reduce forecast toward historical mean (last 10–15 days) by 1–3% per day.  
- For 30-day horizon, if sentiment is mixed or neutral, model often fails to capture short-term volatility; use sentiment-weighted average of 5–7 day moving average to anchor forecast.  
- If true outcome is consistently below model (e.g., 3+ consecutive days), model may be overconfident; reduce forecast by 1–2% per day for next 3–5 days.  
- If sentiment is high and price is falling, model may misread sentiment — forecast should be adjusted downward to reflect “sell-off” sentiment.  
- If model forecast is > 10% above true outcome and sentiment is low, consider “sentiment lag” — model is reacting too early; delay adjustment by 1–2 days.
